findings.where: Article page specimen: the italic pull quote “Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on with a client country!” (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The pull quote is set in the logo blue, which the tile's own palette reserves for links and the button. In the same specimen a link (“Streamlining the PPP Process…”) is also blue. So in an article, blue no longer means 'you can click this': a reader can't tell from colour whether the large blue quote goes somewhere, and on a phone they may tap it and get nothing.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank reader on an article page. They have just seen a blue link and tap the blue quote expecting a source or a related article. Angélique would object too: every post she adds would carry quotes that look like links.

findings.where: Hero: the primary “Get in touch →” button (desktop and phone first screen)
findings.fault: The page's one action is only a mailto link, and Mark's email address appears nowhere in the hero. Visitors who use webmail or have no mail app set up (common on locked-down agency machines) click it and nothing visible happens, or an unconfigured mail app opens. They have no address to copy. The arrow also suggests the button opens a page.
findings.who_objects: A staff member at a multilateral bank on a managed work laptop who clicks “Get in touch”, gets no mail window, and finds no address to copy, so the one thing the homepage wants them to do quietly fails.

findings.fault: “Play again” is a button that replays the animation in place, but it is styled exactly like the underlined blue text links (the lecture link in the article specimen). So the tile teaches one look for two functions, going somewhere and doing something here, and the layout round will inherit that look for in-page controls.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who expects an underlined blue link to open a page and instead sees the heading move. The builder of the layout round would object too, since the tile gives no button style for a secondary in-page action.
